To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
LEKTI fragments inhibit KLK5 activity through a pH-dependent mechanism, leading to desquamation.
LEKTI fragments specifically bind to KLK5, 7 and 14, and that pH-dependent release of the proteases from the LEKTI complex controls desquamation.
LEKTI fragments inhibit KLK5 activity at physiological pH and that this inhibition is relieved at acidic pH, thus allowing KLK5 activity in the most superficial layer of the stratum comeum.

the study of the molecular and cellular mechanisms involved in the pathogenesis of the skin disease known as Netherton syndrome, a severe congenital ichthyosis.
the role of LEKTI in the regulation of the desquamatation process.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

LEKTI fragments are the major inhibitors of KLK5, which are released in the stratum granulosum and the stratum corneal layers, thus controlling KLK5 activity at the appropriate time and location, and thereby the desquamation of corneodesmosomes.
LEKTI fragments are secreted in the epidermal extracellular milieu and specifically target KLK5, which is a key actor of corneodesmosome cleavage in the uppermost stratum corneum layers.
LEKTI controls the desquamation of the stratum comeum by specifically regulating KLK5, 7 and 14 activity through a pH-dependent mechanism.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
(i) LEKTI is cleaved into fragments by furin, (ii) the fragments inhibit KLK5 and KLK7, (iii) the inhibition is pH dependent, and (iv) the pH-dependent inhibition is important for skin homeostasis
LEKTI fragments specifically target and control desquamatory proteases in the epidermal layers, in a pH-dependent manner, and that this process is altered in Netherton syndrome.
the epidermis is able to regulate its desquamation by a pH-dependent mechanism involving LEKTI fragments and KLK5.
The main takeaway from our work is that
LEKTI fragments are the active inhibitors of the KLKs.
LEKTI fragments are the main actors of desquamation, by controlling KLK5 activity in the stratum corneum.
LEKTI, by controlling KLK5 activity through a pH-dependent mechanism, regulates the desquamation and the permeability of the stratum comeum.
